answer.label: Not Edgar Allan Poe — an unsourced internet attribution
answer.authorDates: Anonymous; circulating online as a Poe quote by 2014
answer.sourceLine: No Poe work, letter or recorded remark contains this line. The Poe Museum’s “Did Poe Really Say That?” ↗ (2014) puts it first on its list of fakes, and a 2019 Check Your Fact review rated the attribution “Not credible” ↗. Its real originator is unknown.

source.excerpt: “I wish I could write as mysterious as a cat.”
trail: The Poe Museum’s blog post “Did Poe Really Say That?” ↗ by Chris Semtner (10 September 2014) lists this line first among the fakes. It calls it “one of the most misattributed quotes” and says it “most definitely is not ‘Poe-esque.’”
Check Your Fact ↗ published a fact check of the attribution on 30 June 2019. The CIMPLE claim-review record ↗ of that check gives its rating as “Not credible.”

Poe’s real cat writings are documented by the Poe Society of Baltimore: “The Black Cat” ↗ (1843) and “Instinct vs Reason — A Black Cat” ↗ (Alexander’s Weekly Messenger, 29 January 1840). Neither contains the line.
Writers Write ↗ also calls it a quote “commonly misattributed” to Poe, citing the Poe Museum.
source.excerptNote: The Poe Museum’s verdict: “This is, frustratingly, one of the most misattributed quotes. If you look at the context, the grammar, the style of the quote, it most definitely is not ‘Poe-esque.’”

source.rightsNote: No author or first publication can be identified for this wording, and it does not come from any Poe work. Poe’s own writings are long in the public domain, but that status cannot be extended to an unsourced line falsely credited to him, so no rights status is asserted.

author.name: Edgar Allan Poe
author.heading: The writer it gets pinned on
author.bio: Poe wrote the poem “The Raven,” and his tales of horror and detection helped shape the modern short story. He did write about cats: the 1843 horror tale “The Black Cat” and a short 1840 newspaper sketch, “Instinct vs Reason — A Black Cat.” That record is likely why a cat quote sounds plausible under his name, but this particular line is not in either piece or anywhere else in his writing.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Poe
misattribution.intro: The line spreads on quote sites, merchandise and social-media images under Poe’s name, but nobody who has checked can find it in his writing.

items.why: No Poe source contains the line. The Poe Museum ↗ calls it “one of the most misattributed quotes” and says its context, grammar and style are “most definitely” not Poe’s. Its awkward adjective (“as mysterious” where Poe would have written an adverb) is one sign of this.
Poe’s best-known cat is in his horror tale “The Black Cat” ↗. That connection probably makes a cat quote under his name feel right, but this sentence is not in the story.

misattribution.truthLine: The line has no known author. It is not in Poe’s works, and the Poe Museum ↗ lists it as fake.

context.heading: Poe and cats, for real
lead: Poe did write about cats, which helps explain why this line attaches to him. In 1840 he published a short sketch, “Instinct vs Reason — A Black Cat” ↗, in Alexander’s Weekly Messenger. In 1843 came “The Black Cat” ↗, his tale of a murderer undone by his cat.
The real Poe on cats is darker and more ornate than the internet’s version. Neither text contains a wish to “write as mysterious as a cat.”
context.pull: “Most definitely is not ‘Poe-esque.’” — the Poe Museum
